<reason>High-quality debate that narrowed to one decisive question: does the motion's trigger (repeated *failure*) differ from CON's alternative (penalties for *refusal* after ordered milestones)? PRO's convergence thesis ("CON renamed the motion") was rhetorically powerful, but it depended on reading notice, correction periods, and a good-faith progress defense into the motion's text. CON relentlessly exposed that each such shield converts the trigger from outcome to conduct — i.e., PRO's defensible version of the motion is CON's mechanism, while the motion's distinct content (strict liability on failure) was left undefended. CON named a concrete punished class (the mid-remediation hospital hitting every milestone), supplied a mechanism PRO never engaged (outcome-triggered exposure makes organizations buy legal defensibility before engineering), and turned PRO's own OSHA-abatement analogy into evidence that working penalty regimes punish refusal. PRO's closing asserted ("CON never named one," "don't resolve by vocabulary") rather than answered A4.5/A4.6; CON's closing directly dismantled PRO's final claims. Both sides were disciplined (no fake sourcing, proper Q/A format, one minor clip each), but CON made the decisive clash clearer and resolved it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 into Closing: after PRO (B4.3) imported notice/correction/progress defenses to shield good-faith actors, A4.6 and A5.2 showed those defenses — including PRO's own OSHA correction-order analogy — are refusal-based regimes, so the motion "becomes defensible only by ceasing to be the motion." PRO never squarely answered this; its closing sidestepped into the "vocabulary" frame, which CON's final speech (A5.1) rebutted by naming the extra punished class outright.</best_rebuttal>
